'''''Epilobium hirsutum''''' is a [[flowering plant]] belonging to the willowherb genus ''[[Epilobium]]'' in the family [[Onagraceae]]. It is commonly known as the '''great willowherb''', '''great hairy willowherb''' or '''hairy willowherb'''.<ref name="washington">{{cite web |url=http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/WQ/plants/weeds/willowherb.html |title=Non-native Freshwater Plants: Hairy Willow-Herb |publisher=Washington State Department of Ecology |date=2006 |access-date=6 September 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160921110722/http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/WQ/plants/weeds/willowherb.html |archive-date=21 September 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Local dialectal names include ''codlins and cream'', ''apple pie'' and ''cherry pie''.
[[Image:Epilobium hirsutum - karvane pajulill Keilas.jpg|200px|left|thumb|Close-up of the flowers]]

==Description==
It is a tall, [[perennial]] plant, reaching up to 2 metres in height. The robust [[plant stem|stems]] are profusely hairy with soft spreading hairs.<ref name=Blamey>{{cite book|last1=Blamey|first1=M.|last2=Fitter|first2=R.|last3=Fitter|first3=A|year=2003|title=Wild flowers of Britain and Ireland: The Complete Guide to the British and Irish Flora.|publisher=A & C Black|location=London|isbn=978-1408179505}}</ref>{{rp|160}}<ref>[[Martin, W. Keble]] 1965. ''The New Concise British Flora in Colour''; with nomenclature edited and revised by Douglas H. Kent and foreword by The Duke of Edinburgh. London: Book Club Associates by arrangement with Ebury Press/ Michael Joseph (1982)</ref> The hairy leaves are 2–12 cm long and 0.5–3.5 cm wide. They are long and thin and are widest below the middle. They have sharply toothed edges and no stalk. The large flowers have four notched [[petal]]s. These are purple-pink and are usually 10–16 mm long. There are 8 stamens.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=9780521707725}}</ref>{{rp|357}} The [[carpel|stigma]] is white and has four lobes. The [[sepal]]s are green.

It is relatively easy to distinguish from similar species at least in much of its European range, where its flowers are among species of its genus present there.{{sfn|Strgulc Krajšek|Šegedin|Jogan|2009|p=162}}

==Distribution and habitat==
The native range of the species includes North Africa, most of Europe up to [[Scania|southern Sweden]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/onagra/epilo/epilhir.html|title=Rosendunört, Epilobium hirsutum |language=sv |publisher=Naturhistoriska riksmuseet |date=1997 |access-date=6 September 2016|url-status=dead|archive-date=15 November 1999|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19991115092447/http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/onagra/epilo/epilhir.html}}</ref> and parts of Asia. It is absent from much of [[Scandinavia]] and north-west [[Scotland]]. It has been introduced to North America<ref name="washington" /> and Australia.<ref name="Van Der Kooi 2015" />

It typically grows in wet or damp habitats without dense tree-cover up to 2,500 metres above sea-level. Common habitats include [[marshland]] and the banks of rivers and streams. It also occurs in anthropogenic contexts such as wet ditches and in general in places rich in [[nitrate]]s.{{sfn|Strgulc Krajšek|Šegedin|Jogan|2009|p=162}} It flowers from June to September, with a peak in July and August.<ref name="Van Der Kooi 2015">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| pmid = 25754608| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers| journal = Plant Biology| volume = 18| issue = 1| pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = Van Der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Epilobium hirsutum'' inhabits damp and waste places, river-sides and ditches.<ref>Webb, D.A., Parnell, J. and Doogue, D. 1996. ''An Irish Flora''. Dundalgan Press (W.Tempest) Ltd. Dundalk. {{ISBN|0-85221-131-7}}</ref>

The flowers are visited by many types of insects, and can be characterized by a generalized [[pollination syndrome]].<ref name="Van Der Kooi 2015" /> A number of insects feed on the leaves including the [[Deilephila elpenor|elephant hawkmoth]], ''Deilephila elpenor''.

==Trichomes==
The plant shows glandular [[trichome]]s. They are unicellular, without a specialized basal cell. They have a cutinized cell wall and a protruding pore on the top. The upper part of the trichome cell contains [[flavonoids]], ''e.g.'' [[quercitrin]] and [[myricitrin]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Krajšek | display-authors = etal  | year = 2011 | title = Morphology and glandular activity of unicellular trichomes of Epilobium hirsutum | journal = Biologia Plantarum | volume = 55 | issue = 1| pages = 149–152 | doi=10.1007/s10535-011-0020-z| s2cid = 27328447 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
